question:
Two linear relations are represented by $y=2x+1$ and $y=-x+7$. Their common solution gives the point at which both relations have the same values of $x$ and $y$. A student decides to determine this point using the inverse-matrix method instead of direct substitution. The equations are first rearranged into standard linear form, after which the coefficient matrix is checked for invertibility.

(a) Rewrite the relations as a system in standard form and express it as $AX=B$.

(b) Calculate $|A|$ and justify whether a unique common point exists.

(c) Find $A^{-1}$ and use it to solve for $x$ and $y$.

(d) Verify the solution in both original relations and interpret the result.
explanation:
(a)
The relations can be written as
$$-2x+y=1$$
$$x+y=7$$
Therefore,
$$\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1\\1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\7\end{bmatrix}$$
Thus,
$$A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1\\1 & 1\end{bmatrix},\quad X=\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix},\quad B=\begin{bmatrix}1\\7\end{bmatrix}$$

(b)
$$|A|=(-2)(1)-1(1)=-3$$
Since $|A|=-3\neq0$, the coefficient matrix is invertible and the system has a unique solution. Therefore, the two relations have one common point.

(c)
$$A^{-1}=\frac{1}{-3}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\\-1 & -2\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1\\1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$$
Now,
$$X=A^{-1}B$$
$$X=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1\\1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\7\end{bmatrix}$$
$$X=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-1+7\\1+14\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\5\end{bmatrix}$$
Hence, $x=2$ and $y=5$.

(d)
For the first relation,
$$2(2)+1=5$$
For the second relation,
$$-2+7=5$$
Thus, both relations give $y=5$ when $x=2$. Therefore, their unique common point is $(2,5)$.

options.B:
(a) $\begin{bmatrix}-2&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\7\end{bmatrix}$
(b) $|A|=-3$, so a unique common point exists
(c) $A^{-1}=\frac13\begin{bmatrix}-1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ and $(x,y)=(2,5)$
(d) Both original relations are satisfied, so the unique common point is $(2,5)$
options.D:
(a) $\begin{bmatrix}-2&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\7\end{bmatrix}$
(b) $|A|=0$, so no unique point exists
(c) The inverse does not exist
(d) The two relations have infinitely many common points
